To systematically characterize these dynamics, we integrated single-cell RNA-sequencing data from 21 mouse stroke studies (103 samples; 414,359 cells) spanning multiple models and post-stroke intervals. Using a harmonized computational workflow, we constructed StrokeTime , a single-cell mouse brain atlas covering hyperacute, acute, subacute, and chronic stages post-ischemia. The atlas contains 17 major cell classes and 120 fine-grained transcriptional states within myeloid, lymphoid, vascular, epithelial, neuronal, and glial populations. Myeloid cells showed the greatest plasticity, including disease-associated microglia/macrophage programs shared across resident and infiltrating cells, whereas lymphocytes featured activation and regulatory signatures within lineage constraints. Vascular and mural cells shifted from early inflammatory and barrier-disruptive programs to later fibrotic and angiogenic states. StrokeTime delineates both convergent and cell type-specific injury responses, offering a resource for studying post-ischemic brain immunity, tissue remodeling, and benchmarking future single-cell and single-nucleus studies of cerebrovascular disease.

title: Factor H polymorphism elevates granzyme B and impairs complement inhibition in human and mouse models
abstract: The complement factor H (CFH) Y402H polymorphism is a leading genetic risk factor for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Here, we identify extracellular granzyme B (GzmB) as a crucial mediator connecting complement dysregulation to structural pathology. In non-AMD human donor eyes, the high-risk CFH genotype was associated with increased GzmB-positive choroidal mast cells, membrane attack complex deposition, and distinct vitronectin redistribution. Using in vitro human retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, we demonstrate that complement fragment C5a triggers GzmB secretion and zonula occludens-1 disruption. RNA sequencing of GzmB-stimulated RPE cells confirmed transcriptomic signatures of barrier dysfunction and cellular stress. Furthermore, GzmB-deficient mice displayed preserved choroidal vitronectin compared with wild-type controls, supporting a role for GzmB in cleaving this terminal complement inhibitor. These findings delineate a pathogenic C5a-GzmB pathway compromising extracellular matrix integrity, implicating extracellular GzmB as a critical downstream mediator linking genetic risk to early AMD onset.

title: Screening colorectal tumor-associated fibroblasts using dual-channel THz biosensor
abstract: In clinical oncology, label-free identification of colorectal tumor-associated fibroblast (CAF) subtypes is challenging. In this work, a terahertz (THz) metasurface exhibiting dual channels of probation, quasi-bound states in the continuum (q-BICs) and electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT), is used to screen CAF subtypes in colorectal tumors. When impinging light is polarized along x axis, the pro-tumorigenic myofibroblasts (myCAFs) cause frequency red-shift of q-BIC resonances compared to intestinal epithelial cells, while anti-tumorigenic antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs) result in blueshift. Similarly, for EIT modes, when light is polarized along the orthogonal polarization, myCAFs result in a frequency red-shift while apCAFs result in blueshift. These frequency shifts are attributed to the dielectric environment variation due to the surface hall-marks of CAFs. To validate our results, we conducted flow cytometry and gene expression analyses that confirmed distinct hallmarks of myCAFs and apCAFs, consistent with the resonance frequency shifts observed in THz metasurface measurements. Our findings demonstrate a label-free and cost-effective method for screening CAF subtypes using two-parameters—q-BICs and EIT—which can help speed up cancer diagnosis.

title: IgM monoclonal antibodies reduce IgG-mediated antibody-dependent enhancement of Zika and dengue virus infectivity
abstract: Summary Zika virus (ZIKV) is an arthropod-borne flavivirus endemic to Latin America and Africa for which IgG-mediated antibody-dependent enhancement of infectivity (ADE) is a phenomenon of concern. The interplay dynamics between flavivirus-specific antibodies of the IgG and IgM isotypes are mostly unknown. Here, we used DH1017.IgM, a previously described human-derived, pentameric, ultrapotent neutralizing ZIKV IgM monoclonal antibody (mAb) and a recombinantly produced IgM version of neutralizing EDE1 mAb C8 (C8.IgM) to assess if IgM antibodies can interfere with IgG-mediated ADE in vitro . Both mAbs consistently reduced IgG-mediated ADE across a panel of ZIKV-binding IgG mAbs in a dose-dependent manner. ADE mitigation was achieved at DH1017.IgM sub-neutralizing concentrations. C8.IgM also mitigated IgG-mediated ADE against the whole panel, demonstrating generalizability. Finally, DH1017.IgM confirmed inhibition of ADE at sub-neutralizing concentrations in sera of ZIKV-infected individuals. In conclusion, mAbs of the IgM isotype may potently counter the adverse effects of IgG-mediated ADE.

title: Non-invasive glycemic control leveraging ultrasound dose window activation of MscL in diabetic mice
abstract: Type 2 diabetes is characterized by impaired glucose homeostasis and progressive pancreatic β cell dysfunction, highlighting the need for externally controllable strategies for metabolic regulation. Here, we combined low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) with the mechanosensitive channel MscL-G22S to establish a tunable sonogenetic system for glucose regulation. Graded ultrasound stimulation was evaluated in MscL-G22S-expressing β cells and diabetic db/db mice to define an effective acoustic dose range. Within an intermediate dose window, LIPUS increased intracellular Ca 2+ levels and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in vitro and improved glycemic control, insulin sensitivity, islet morphology, and systemic metabolic profiles in vivo . Serum metabolomics further identified metabolic pathway alterations associated with combined LIPUS and MscL-G22S activation. These findings establish a quantitative framework for relating ultrasound dose to sonogenetic metabolic responses and support further investigation of ultrasound-controlled regulation of glucose homeostasis.

title: Contralateral delay activity during dynamic spatial updates in working memory
abstract: Working memory (WM) enables us to maintain and directly manipulate mental representations, yet we know little about the neural implementation of this privileged online format. We recorded electroencephalography data as human subjects engaged in a task requiring continuous updates to the locations of objects retained in WM as well as in a visually identical task with WM demands removed. Analysis of neural data suggested WM-related contralateral delay activity reversed polarity as objects held in WM moved to the opposite hemifield. The control task suggested this was partially but not fully explained by visual attention demands. Thus, the spatial location of activity related to both attention and WM was updated to meet behavioral demands as the spatial location of remembered objects changed.

title: NDUFS1 promotes malignant breast cancer behaviors through enhancement of mitochondrial respiration and PROX1/c-Myc signaling
abstract: Cancer cells exploit oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) for growth and metastasis. NDUFS1, the largest subunit of the electron transport chain complex I, is a promising therapeutic target in cancer but has a context-dependent role. Here, we elucidate the function of NDUFS1 in breast cancer. Elevated NDUFS1 expression was associated with advanced breast cancer stage and poor survival outcomes. In vitro experiments showed that NDUFS1 knockdown inhibited breast cancer cell proliferation, invasion, and stemness-associated properties, whereas NDUFS1 overexpression enhanced these phenotypes. Moreover, NDUFS1 directly regulated mitochondrial respiratory function in breast cancer cells and increased c-Myc expression via PROX1. In a mouse model of breast cancer, NDUFS1 knockdown in injected mammary carcinoma cells or OXPHOS inhibition decreased tumor growth and PROX1 and c-Myc expression. Our study highlights the role of the NDUFS1-PROX1-c-Myc axis in breast cancer progression, paving the way for new therapies targeting breast cancer mitochondrial OXPHOS.

title: SGK1 mediates TGF-β1-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition and fibrosis in experimental bronchiolitis obliterans
abstract: Bronchiolitis obliterans (BO) represents a major complication limiting long-term survival after lung transplantation, with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) serving as a core pathogenic mechanism. The TGF-β1 signaling pathway plays a critical role in EMT induction and can activate serum/glucocorticoid-regulated kinase 1 (SGK1) expression. While SGK1 is upregulated in various fibrotic diseases, its functional significance in BO remains undefined. To elucidate SGK1's role in post-transplant BO fibrosis and its interaction with the TGF-β1 pathway, we established a murine heterotopic tracheal transplantation model. Histopathological evaluation and RNA sequencing demonstrated significant SGK1 upregulation in BO lesions by day 28. In vitro , both pharmacological inhibition (EMD638683) and genetic knockdown of SGK1 (siRNA) attenuated TGF-β1-induced EMT in the human small airway epithelial cell line (HSAECs), while concurrently suppressing the expression of extracellular matrix genes (COL1 and FN1). Furthermore, SGK1 inhibition reduced TGF-β1-induced SMAD2/3 phosphorylation. Therapeutic administration of EMD638683, initiated after disease establishment, significantly ameliorated BO pathology. These findings demonstrate that SGK1 promotes BO-associated fibrosis through TGF-β1-mediated EMT and ECM deposition, identifying SGK1 as a potential therapeutic target for post-transplant BO intervention.

title: Hippocampal and hypothalamic cell-type specific mechanisms underlying nutritional and metabolic modulation of Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Background: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a pervasive neurodegenerative disorder with hallmarks of beta-amyloid (Aβ) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. Considering the suboptimal benefit of Aβ clearing drugs, the association between metabolic disorders and AD provides an alternative angle to understand the role of metabolic dysfunction in AD pathogenesis and the potential of modulating metabolism for therapeutic development. Methods: We investigated the effects of metabolic modulators, namely, high fructose consumption as a potential risk, and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and nicotinamide riboside (NR) as potentially beneficial, on cell type specific transcriptomic responses in the hippocampus and hypothalamus of the 5xFAD mouse model featuring advanced Aβ plaques. Findings: Fructose-induced metabolic syndrome increased expression of complement component 3 in ependymal cells and inflammatory genes in microglia, which were normalized by DHA and NR. NR and DHA led to reversals of Aβ-associated transcriptional signatures across cell types, but the effects were modified by fructose. DHA and NR also both reversed the loss of hippocampal oligodendrocytes in AD, with DHA further reducing hippocampal microglia and increasing hypothalamic astrocytes and NR further increasing hippocampal neuronal proportions. Interpretation: Our study supports the impact of metabolic regulation on AD-associated cell types and pathways and provides molecular support for utilizing nutritional modulators for AD intervention.

title: Early-warning signals of critical transitions in global ecoregions
abstract: Terrestrial ecoregions represent coherent ecological units shaped by shared environmental conditions and biological communities. As ecosystems approach critical transitions, their resilience declines, showing slower recovery from perturbations and increasing temporal autocorrelation. Here, we analyze 22 years of global satellite vegetation data to detect early warning signals of structural ecological change across all terrestrial ecoregions. By combining spatial clustering, vegetation trend analysis, and resilience indicators, we identify ecoregions exhibiting both vegetation change and declining resilience. We find that approximately one-quarter of ecoregions, covering over one-third of Earth's land surface, show consistent signals of emerging structural transitions. Many of these occur in regions with low direct human modification, suggesting a strong role for large-scale environmental drivers. The detected patterns reveal increasing internal fragmentation within ecoregions and highlight regions potentially approaching critical transitions. This framework provides a scalable approach for identifying ecosystems at risk and supports targeted monitoring and conservation planning.

title: Developmental mechanism and evolutionary process of cephalopod suckers
abstract: In contrast to animals possessing clear modularity such as vertebrates and arthropods, the evolution of novel structures in animals with indistinct body modules, like molluscs, remains poorly understood. Among molluscs, cephalopods have unique arms and suckers, which are particularly notable because they show clear modularity despite their derivation from a simple flat foot of the ancestral molluscs. However, their developmental mechanisms and evolutionary processes have yet to be revealed. Gene expression analyses of cephalopod arms and gastropod feet showed that well-known appendage patterning genes in animals with clear modularity were expressed in cephalopod arms and gastropod feet but not in suckers. Instead, genes such as Ets1 , typically involved in early embryonic processes like gastrulation in molluscs, were specifically expressed in suckers. These results suggest that cephalopod arms recruited developmental mechanisms similar to segmented appendages, whereas suckers represent a cephalopod-specific innovation formed through the co-option of genes contributing to early embryogenesis.

title: Diet-attributable vascular/metabolic disease burden comparisons and public health implications in Western Europe and North America
abstract: Ischemic heart disease (IHD), ischemic stroke (IS), type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and lower-extremity vascular disease are leading causes of disability in Western Europe and North America, but their diet-attributable burden remains unclear. Using Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 data, we assessed the association between the Socio-demographic Index (SDI) and the vascular/metabolic disease burden and compared the cross-regional burden through multi-dimensional time-trend, risk contribution, and projection analyses. Mendelian randomization (MR) tested causal diet effects on disease subtypes. Frontier analysis showed diet-related IHD and IS burden declined with SDI, while T2DM increased. By 2023, Western Europe had a lower burden than North America. Processed meat and whole grain dominated T2DM and IHD burden, respectively. Joinpoint analysis revealed declining trends. Projections to 2035 indicated North America remains higher. MR identified several potential causal links. This study provides a basis for vascular/metabolic disease prevention policies and dietary interventions in Western Europe and North America.

title: Dopamine dynamics promote cooperative behavior not just the rewards accompanying cooperation
abstract: Cooperation requires precise spatiotemporal coordination, whereas previous studies have largely focused on decision-making neural circuits. We combined the genetically encoded dopamine (DA) sensor GRAB DA3m with a cooperative nose-poke task to monitor DA dynamics in the medial shell of the nucleus accumbens (NAcmedSh) during cooperative learning and maintenance in mice. Fiber photometry revealed that cooperation-related DA transients gradually increased during learning and strongly correlated with cooperative success. In non-cooperative social and independent controls, DA signals were associated with reward delivery. Extinction and delayed-reward experiments dissociated cooperation-related DA activity from external rewards. Reversal experiments showed that this representation remained stable after task switching. Furthermore, local microinjection of the D1 receptor antagonist SCH-23390 (0.05 μg/side) into the NAc selectively reduced cooperative success without affecting feeding motivation or locomotor activity. These findings indicate that NAc DA signaling represents the intrinsic value of cooperation beyond external reward, with D1R-dependent phasic DA contributing to its maintenance.

title: Variance of human cortical synaptic transmission inferred from non-invasive magnetoencephalography of somatosensory evoked population spikes
abstract: Non-invasive recordings of somatosensory evoked brain responses (SERs) contain high-frequency (∼600 Hz) evoked responses (hfSERs) which can be recorded at the single-trial level using ultralow-noise magnetoencephalography (MEG). hfSERs were shown to represent cortical population spikes and consist of an early (pre-synaptic) and a late (post-synaptic) component. Here, a statistical model of cortical population spiking reproduced single-trial hfSERs evoked by median-nerve stimulation in 5 healthy subjects. hfSERs were best replicated when variability was added only to the late (post-synaptic) model component, explaining 85% of inter-trial variability across subjects. Adding variability also to the early (pre-synaptic) component caused overfitting in most subjects, yet still indicated larger amplitude and latency variability post-synaptically. This proof-of-concept establishes model-based inference from non-invasively recorded population spikes as a means to estimate synaptic transmission variability in human neocortex. The approach opens a route to studying synaptic function in health and disease where invasive recordings are unavailable.

title: GFAP mutants cause imbalance of selective lipid classes in a cellular model of Alexander disease
abstract: Alexander disease (AxD) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder caused by mutations in glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), primarily affecting astrocytes. Although these mutations alter astrocyte structure and metabolism, their impact on the lipidome remains understudied. Here, wild-type GFP-GFAP and AxD-associated mutants (R239C, R239G, R79C, and E373K) were expressed in U-87 MG astrocytoma cells to evaluate GFAP organization through confocal microscopy and lipidomic alterations quantified by mass spectrometry. Membrane fluidity and lipid storage were complementarily assessed. Expression of AxD-associated GFAP mutants induced distinct lipidomic alterations, with R239C eliciting the most pronounced changes, including enrichment of sphingomyelins, trihexosylceramides, acylcarnitines, triglycerides, cholesteryl esters, and ether-linked lipids. These alterations suggest adaptive mechanisms to preserve membrane integrity, lipid raft organization, bioenergetics, redox homeostasis, and cell survival. Overall, in the AxD astrocytoma cell model, different GFAP mutations induce extensive and non-overlapping remodeling of lipids involved in membrane structure and organization, antioxidant defense, and bioenergetic pathways.

title: Endogenous targets of Zuo1-mediated mRNA surveillance encode proteins with higher predicted disorder
abstract: Zuo1 slows elongating ribosomes in response to nascent peptide misfolding, which in turn triggers co-translational decay of the transcript. The endogenous substrates of this pathway have remained undefined. Using RNA-sequencing and ribosome profiling of unstressed wild-type and zuo1Δ cells, we identified transcripts that accumulate in the absence of Zuo1, representing mRNAs normally downregulated by Zuo1-mediated surveillance. Proteins encoded by these transcripts displayed higher predicted disorder across multiple metrics, were enriched in basic residues, were depleted of proline residues, and were shorter in length. Ribosome profiling revealed that Zuo1 target transcripts exhibited higher ribosome occupancy in the presence of Zuo1, and the ratio of wild-type to zuo1Δ ribosome occupancy positively correlated with predicted disorder. These findings indicate that Zuo1 surveillance acts preferentially on transcripts encoding nascent chains that fail to acquire stable structure.

title: Research on regulation method for suppression of pantograph-catenary arc by airflow in low-pressure environment
abstract: The Pantograph-Catenary (P-C) arc is a common phenomenon in the P-C current collection system. System faults caused by P-C arcs are the main factor affecting the safe and stable operation of trains. With the extension of global rail transit to plateau areas, the problem of frequent P-C arc in a low-pressure environment needs to be solved urgently. Therefore, the MHD model of P-C arc regulation in a low-pressure environment is established, and the influence of longitudinal airflow on the arc's dynamic characteristics is studied. Findings indicate that longitudinal airflow can effectively suppress the arc drift phenomenon of P-C arcs. Moreover, the arc is easier to regulate effectively with decreasing air pressure, and the control effect can reach 100%. In addition, longitudinal airflow can reduce the arc temperature. The optimal airflow speeds for longitudinal airflow regulation at different air pressures are obtained. A testing platform for P-C arc regulation is built. The effect of longitudinal airflow on arc drift regulation is verified, and it is found that airflow regulation can also effectively reduce the ablation failure on electrodes caused by the arc. This study provides theoretical guidance for improving the service life of the P-C system.

title: Communicative diversity scales with social network structure in bottlenose dolphins
abstract: Social relationships can shape the demands placed on animal communication, but different dimensions of social organization may affect signal repertoires in different ways. We investigated whether variation in social network structure covaried with whistle repertoire organization in wild common bottlenose dolphins ( Tursiops truncatus ). We combined photo-identification and concurrent acoustic recordings across two field seasons, quantified group social topology and bond-strength structure, and characterized whistle repertoires using Hill diversity and continuous acoustic-distance metrics. Elastic-net models showed that groups with higher clustering coefficients had lower repertoire diversity, whereas mean and variable bond strength were associated with acoustic-distance structure. These relationships persisted after accounting for predominant behavioral state and group size. Our findings indicate that social cohesion and relationship heterogeneity correspond to distinct dimensions of communicative organization, supporting a multidimensional view of social and vocal complexity in fission-fusion societies.

title: ELAVL1 overexpression potentiates cervical cancer malignancy via regulating the ACVRL1/CASP14 pathway
abstract: Cervical cancer is the fourth common gynecological malignancy. To explore new therapeutic targets, we found that the transcriptional and translational levels of ELAVL1 were markedly increased in SiHa and HeLa cells as well as cervical cancer specimens. Knockdown of ELAVL1 substantially suppressed the proliferation, invasion, and migration of cervical cancer cells, while inducing apoptosis. Conversely, overexpression of ELAVL1 resulted in a substantial increase in the proliferative, invasive, and migratory capacities of SiHa cells. Bioinformatics predictions, RIP-qPCR and dual-luciferase reporter assays indicated that ELAVL1 might interact with the 3′UTR of ACVRL1 , and upregulate ACVRL1 and CASP14 expression. Co-transfection experiments and functional assays revealed that ELAVL1 might modulate malignant phenotypes of cervical cancer cells via the ACVRL1/CASP14 pathway. Furthermore, in vivo si-ELAVL1 administration significantly inhibited tumor growth in nude mouse xenograft models. ELAVL1 may promote cervical cancer progression, potentially through regulating the ACVRL1/CASP14 pathway, rendering ELAVL1 a potential candidate for therapeutic intervention.

title: Deep learning based detection of active pulmonary tuberculosis from chest radiographs in a retrospective prospective multicenter study
abstract: Active tuberculosis remains a major global health problem, and distinguishing active from non-active disease on chest radiographs could accelerate triage where radiology resources are limited. We developed ShuffleNetV2 using 4,613 radiographs from two centers and evaluated it in retrospective external (1,318 patients) and prospective (560 patients) cohorts. The model achieved AUCs of 0.917 and 0.896, respectively, and performance was stable across prespecified demographic and scanner subgroups. In the prospective cohort, artificial-intelligence assistance increased radiologist AUCs to 0.897-0.937 across experience levels. These findings support ShuffleNetV2 as a rapid decision-support tool for prioritizing confirmatory clinical and microbiological assessment; positive predictions should not be used alone to initiate treatment.

title: Bacteroides fragilis outer membrane vesicle mediates Pseudomonadota colonization by inducing autophagy on the skin
abstract: Skin homeostasis is essential for host defense. Though constantly exposed to the external environment, signals from anaerobes have been detected in deeper skin layers, with their functional role in cutaneous immunity remaining unclear. Here, we explored whether skin-associated Bacteroidota contribute to pathogen exclusion via host autophagy. Comparative analysis of the skin microbiota revealed a progressive reduction in Pseudomonadota abundance alongside an increase in Bacteroidota during childhood-to-adulthood transition. A significant inverse correlation between Bacteroidota and Pseudomonadota abundance was observed in pediatric cohorts. Bacteroides fragilis and its secreted outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) induced autophagy, which facilitated Pseudomonadota clearance in macrophages. In vivo colonization experiments showed that live B. fragilis bacteria or intact OMVs outcompeted Pseudomonadota in wild-type mice, but not in lc3a −/− mice. These findings provide a plausible model explaining the inverse association detected in human cohorts, indicating that B. fragilis may help suppress potentially pathogenic taxa like Pseudomonadota on the skin.

title: Modulation of mGluR1 signaling improves Purkinje cell dysfunction associated with spinocerebellar ataxia 14
abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 14 (SCA14) is caused by mutations in protein kinase C gamma (PKCγ) that lead to constitutive kinase activity and Purkinje cell dysfunction in the cerebellum. PKCγ acts downstream of metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (mGluR1) signaling; however, it remains unclear whether alterations in this upstream pathway contribute to the cellular defects induced by mutant PKCγ. Here, we investigated the role of mGluR1 signaling in PKCγ-dependent pathology using organotypic cerebellar slice cultures from a mouse model of SCA14. Modulation of mGluR1 signaling partially improved dendritic abnormalities and dendritic spine phenotypes associated with constitutive PKCγ activation. In addition, inhibition of mGluR1 reduced phosphorylation of PKC substrates and restored the enrichment of scaffold proteins and their synaptic proximity to mGluR1. Together, our results demonstrate that mGluR1 signaling contributes to Purkinje cell abnormalities induced by constitutive PKCγ activity and that modulation of mGluR1 can improve disease-associated cellular phenotypes in SCA14.

title: CXCR5 regulates CD8+/GZMB+ T cell infiltration and apoptotic signaling in breast cancer
abstract: Emerging evidence associates CXCR5 expression with immunotherapy outcomes; however, the intrinsic role of tumor-derived CXCR5 in modulating chemo-immunotherapy sensitivity in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains uncharacterized. This study was conducted using murine 4T1 and human MDA-MB-231 TNBC models. Tumor cell CXCR5 expression was manipulated through overexpression or shRNA-mediated silencing. Therapeutic efficacy of paclitaxel (PTX, 10 mg/kg)±Tislelizumab (TIS, 10 mg/kg) was evaluated using in vivo tumor models and T cell cytotoxicity assays. We demonstrated that combination therapy effectively suppressed 4T1 tumor growth, extended survival, and enhanced intratumoral CD8 + /GZMB + T cell infiltration coupled with increased cleaved-caspase-3 activation in murine studies. In vitro analyses revealed that CXCR5-high MDA-MB-231 cells exhibited heightened sensitivity to T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity in combination with PTX+TIS, corresponding with decreased BCL2 expression and elevated BAX levels. Our findings establish tumor-intrinsic CXCR5 as a pivotal determinant of chemo-immunotherapy efficacy in TNBC, mechanistically linked to enhanced CD8 + T cell infiltration and apoptotic signaling.

title: A fibril-selective single-domain antibody targets pathogenic amyloid-β assemblies and protects human neurons
abstract: Alzheimer disease is characterized by extracellular amyloid-β deposition that contributes to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Although anti-amyloid-β antibodies reduce plaque burden, their use requires monitoring for amyloid-related imaging abnormalities. Here, phage display against immobilized Aβ40 fibrils representing a patient-relevant polymorph identified J8, a fibril-selective, Fc-free single-domain antibody. J8 bound fibrils with high apparent affinity, showed no detectable binding to monomeric Aβ40, decorated fibril surfaces, and recognized plaque-associated amyloid in Alzheimer disease brain tissue. During concurrent fibril exposure, J8 reduced apoptotic signaling in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and forebrain organoids. Single-nucleus profiling of pooled organoids identified fibril-associated stress programs and opposite-direction expression patterns in the FibJ8 condition; fibril-associated changes showed the strongest directional concordance with advanced disease pathology. These findings identify J8 as a fibril-selective candidate and support organoid-based evaluation of anti-amyloid reagents as a fit-for-purpose preclinical tool.

title: Multivariate connectivity deviations reveal task-evoked and clinical network reorganization
abstract: Abstract Understanding how cognitive demands and pathology reshape large-scale functional connectivity (FC) requires methods that are both multivariate and region-specific. Here we introduce One-class SVM-based Connectome Anomaly Recognition (OSCAR), a normative modelling framework that detects condition-related deviations in the multivariate connectivity profile of a brain region. OSCAR learns the distribution of region-to-whole-brain connectivity patterns given a reference state sample (e.g. resting-state data; RS) using a one-class support vector machine (OCSVM). The trained models are then applied to FC profiles from a target condition (e.g., task or patient group). The outlier proportions are used to quantify the difference between the reference and target condition. We validated OSCAR on three diverse tasks and a patient cohort with early psychosis. OSCAR consistently identified condition-sensitive regions in networks known to support conflict processing, object-location memory, lexical learning, and early psychosis, respectively, including thalamic and basal ganglia regions. Moreover, it detected additional well-established task– or disease-relevant parcels not captured by the comparison method permutation-based multivariate analysis of variance (perMANOVA). Regions flagged by OSCAR were at least as close, and often closer, to independent task-activation findings than those identified by perMANOVA. These results demonstrate that OSCAR provides an interpretable, region-centred normative modelling approach that is sensitive to subtle multivariate FC deviations, and offers a practical tool for mapping condition-specific reconfigurations of functional brain networks with high external validity, in both experimental and clinical settings.

title: Biotin-dependent metabolism controls germinal center fate and vaccine-induced antibody diversification
abstract: Nutrient availability shapes antibody responses, yet its role in metabolic checkpoints governing germinal center (GC) B-cell differentiation remains incompletely defined. Using heterozygous (HZ) Slc5a6 M60K mice modeling human loss-of-function mutations in the multivitamin transporter SLC5A6, we found that deficient biotin imports impaired mitochondrial metabolism and restricted preGC-to-dark zone progression after vaccination. Single-cell transcriptomics and RNA velocity revealed disrupted GC trajectories, while B-cell receptor repertoire analysis showed impaired class-switch recombination, somatic hypermutation, and vaccine-induced clonal diversity. Spatial multiplexed imaging showed reduced GL7-high GC-associated B-cell regions. Flow cytometric analyses revealed reduced frequencies of RBD-specific B cells and RBD-specific GL7 + CD95 + GC B cells in HZ mice, with higher frequencies after biotin supplementation. Pseudovirus assays demonstrated impaired neutralization of Wuhan-Hu-1 and Omicron BA.2. Dietary biotin supplementation restored GC-associated differentiation, antibody diversification, and vaccine-induced humoral responses. These findings identify biotin-dependent mitochondrial metabolism as an important checkpoint linking micronutrient availability to GC B-cell differentiation and vaccine responsiveness.

title: A twentieth-century shift in psoriasis age at onset toward a metabolically associated phenotype
abstract: Psoriasis, long regarded as a chronic immune-mediated skin disorder, is now recognized as a systemic inflammatory disease linked to metabolic dysfunction. Whether this link is intrinsic to the disease or a consequence of recent environmental change bears on how psoriasis is understood. We reconstructed the epidemiology of psoriasis from the early twentieth century onward, combining archival and citation-chain searches, logistic-growth modeling of historical prevalence, and Gaussian-mixture modeling of reconstructed age-at-onset data from pre- and post-World War II cohorts. Before the war, psoriasis arose in adolescents and young adults without metabolic comorbidity; over subsequent decades the age-at-onset distribution shifted toward older ages, and a middle-age-onset group associated with cardiometabolic disease became prominent, paralleling the population-wide rise of metabolic disease. We found no robust evidence that psoriasis itself became more frequent. These observational, hypothesis-generating findings are consistent with a shared environmental contribution to psoriasis and metabolic disease.

title: Single-cell transcriptomics reveals reversible microglia/macrophage activation after human retinal neuron transplantation into mouse retina
abstract: ABSTRACT The host retinal microglia and macrophage activation remains a major challenge for the integration of donor neurons following transplantation. Previously, we and others have shown that it is possible to increase donor retinal ganglion cell (RGC) survival by inhibiting the microglia-RGC interaction with Annexin V or through reprogramming microglia with the soluble Fas ligand. However, the exact mechanisms of the microglia/macrophage activation and their heterogeneity following transplantation remain unknown. To address this question, the donor RGC were differentiated from Brn3b-Tdtomato-Thy1.2 human embryonic stem cells using a 3D protocol, followed by dissociation and RGC purification. RGC were delivered subretinally (1.5x10 4 viable cells/eye) into 3-6-month-old CX3CR1 GFP knock-in mice. Three days after transplantation retinas were dissociated into single-cell suspension and GFP-positive myeloid cells isolated using FACS. Of the sorted cells, up to 10,000 viable cells per sample were used for single-cell RNA library preparation and sequenced using the 10X Genomics Chromium platform. In addition, several retinas were fixed and stained for donor RGC (mCherry) and host microglia/macrophages (Iba1). RNA Velocity was used to reconstruct the myeloid cell population and activation trajectory from scRNAseq data. We observed continuous bi-directional transition of microglia/macrophages from a homeostatic to an activated state. We also observed that the response to the transplant falls into the classic disease-associated-microglia (DAM) activation paradigm with a decrease in expression of the homeostatic gene Tmem119 and an increase in expression of disease-associated genes including Apoe, Lgals3, and Spp1 . Our findings show that the host retinal myeloid cell population undergoes activation upon transplantation of stem-cell derived donor RGC, with a molecular profile of the activated cells similar to that of activated myeloid cells associated with neurodegenerative diseases of the brain and the eye. Advanced integrated transcriptomic analysis shows separate activated-to-homeostatic and homeostatic-to-activated trajectories suggesting the reversibility of this process.

title: Comparative efficacy and safety of low dose vs. standard-dose immune checkpoint inhibitors: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Several studies have reported that low-dose of programmed cell death-1 (PD-1)/programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitors is effective. However, it is unknown whether the efficacy of low dose is as effective as standard dose. We compared the efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor at different doses as a single agent for patients with solid tumors. We searched published clinical trials with the clinical outcomes of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor until December 1, 2024. The low dose is defined as lower than the dose approved by FDA. A total of 1,084 patients from 14 studies were included in the analysis. The pooled analysis of seven studies demonstrated no significant difference in overall survival (OS) between the low dose and standard dose of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor. Safety evaluations from five studies indicated no significant differences in adverse events (AEs). Our study indicated that low dose of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor as monotherapy can provide comparable efficacy and safety to standard dose in patients with solid tumors.

title: Neuroplastic changes in functional connectivity associated with problematic smartphone use in a data-driven rs-fMRI study
abstract: Previous studies revealed altered functional connections in problematic smartphone use (PSU), but most of the studies used self-reported data to assess PSU. Therefore, in the current study, we investigated neuroplastic changes in functional connectivity (FC) associated with PSU and objectively measured smartphone screen time (OMST) using data-driven multivariate pattern analysis. Based on our results, OMST had no direct effect on FC, but the FC between the somatomotor and the frontoparietal networks was negatively, while the connection between the somatomotor and limbic networks was positively associated with PSU. In addition, the FC between the default mode network and the limbic system was negatively, while connectivity between the default mode and the somatomotor networks was also negatively associated with PSU. In light of our findings, PSU may impair higher level brain networks, although future studies are highly needed to determine which specific objectively measured screen time activities might affect brain functions.

title: Prussian blue electrocatalyst in bioanalysis: From oxidase biosensors to peroxidase kinetics assays
abstract: Prussian blue (PB) has evolved as the most advantageous electrocatalyst for preparing H 2 O 2 biosensors due to its exceptional high sensitivity and specificity, which are vital to minimizing the interferences in complex biological samples. However, the widespread adoption of PB-based bioanalysis has been severely restricted by its inherent instability in neutral and alkaline environments, compromising the measurement accuracy and reliability. This review provides an overview of the strategies used to improve PB stability in bioanalysis, such as integration with carbon nanomaterials, polymer encapsulation (e.g., Nafion and chitosan), and transition metal ion (e.g., Ni, Co)-doping. Furthermore, we comprehensively cover the bioanalytical applications of PB: from traditional oxidase-based biosensors to emerging high-impact applications enabled by the enhanced PB stability. These includ real-time H 2 O 2 quantification in tumors and brain tissue, electrochemical immunosensing, and kinetics assays for peroxidases and peroxygenases acting on insoluble substrates.

title: SH3YL1-TLR5 complex-mediated vicious cycle contributes to FSGS pathogenesis
abstract: The mechanisms underlying focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), particularly podocyte damage, remain unclear. We found that patients with FSGS have significantly elevated serum and urine levels of SH3YL1, especially in more severe cases. Adriamycin stimulates SH3YL1 secretion, which induces proinflammatory cytokines and enhances podocyte injury. The receptor for secreted SH3YL1 is identified as Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5), with the ectodomain specifically binding SH3YL1 at an affinity of 1.49 × 10 −8 M. In murine FSGS model, knockout of TLR5 or SH3YL1 alleviated renal inflammation, podocyte damage, sclerosis, and tubular injury. The proposed mechanism involves a vicious cycle where renal injury induces SH3YL1 secretion, promoting podocyte death and local inflammation, which further amplifies SH3YL1 secretion. We developed a therapeutic antibody that neutralizes secreted SH3YL1, effectively reducing podocyte death and sclerosis. These findings suggest that the SH3YL1-TLR5 axis drives podocyte damage in FSGS and that the antibody could serve as a promising therapeutic intervention.

title: Temporal dynamics of antennal responses encode plant stress and ecological relevance in Spodoptera littoralis moths
abstract: Polyphagous insects draw fitness-relevant information from complex plant odor blends, yet electroantennography (EAG) studies often emphasize response amplitude rather than temporal structure. We combined natural plant volatile stimuli, temporal EAG analysis, and machine-learning classification to examine the responses of male and female Spodoptera littoralis antennae to host/edible plants, non-hosts, and drought-stressed plants. EAGs entailed much information about plant volatiles. Female responses showed stronger functional organization and higher classification performance for the above-mentioned categories, particularly for non-host plants, whereas males retained discrimination only under high-contrast stress conditions. These findings suggest that peripheral antennal dynamics preserve biologically relevant information about plant suitability and physiological state. More broadly, this framework offers a new approach for linking peripheral olfactory physiology with future electrophysiological and behavioral experiments.

title: Vagal maneuvers and pharmacological cardioversion in stable PSVT: A systematic review with implications for emergency nursing practice
abstract: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) is a common arrhythmic emergency for which vagal maneuvers offer a non-pharmacological route to cardioversion before drug escalation. This systematic review compared the effectiveness and safety of vagal maneuvers-particularly the standard and modified Valsalva maneuvers-against pharmacological cardioversion in adults with stable PSVT. Following PRISMA 2020 guidance, eleven studies published between 2014 and 2024 were identified across six databases and synthesized narratively owing to clinical and methodological heterogeneity. The modified Valsalva maneuver consistently achieved higher cardioversion rates than the standard technique and carotid sinus massage, with a favorable safety profile, while adenosine remained effective but more frequently associated with recurrence and discomfort. Effectiveness varied by age, arrhythmia subtype, and care setting. Collectively, the evidence supports the modified Valsalva maneuver as a safe, low-cost, first-line option before pharmacological escalation, with particular relevance to nurse-led management in emergency and prehospital care.

title: Artificial intelligence across the gastric cancer care continuum: Clinical evidence, multimodal integration, and translation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across the gastric cancer care continuum, but its clinical maturity differs substantially among endoscopy, cross-sectional imaging, digital pathology, prognostic modeling, treatment selection, and surgical support. Existing reviews have often focused on individual modalities or summarized algorithmic performance without systematically distinguishing technical feasibility from translational readiness. We conducted a structured narrative review of studies indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE and the Web of Science Core Collection from January 2022 through July 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking. Earlier landmark studies were retained when necessary to explain the development of major applications. Priority was given to prospective, multicenter, externally validated, and clinically actionable studies. Evidence maturity was assessed according to study design, validation breadth, workflow relevance, calibration and clinical-utility assessment, and implementation evidence. The main constraint on gastric cancer AI is no longer pattern-recognition capability but the absence of reproducible clinical benefit under real-world conditions. Priorities include multiregional prospective validation, standardized calibration and decision curve assessment, comparison of clinicians with and without AI, integration into existing workflows, evaluation of economic and patient-level outcomes, and post-deployment monitoring.

title: Greenery or fear: Site use of Himalayan ibex in a predator-dominant landscape
abstract: ), has increased in abundance alongside snow leopard populations due to ongoing conservation efforts. However, the behavioral strategies that enable ibex to persist in the predator-rich mountain ecosystems of Pakistan remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we investigated habitat use and co-occurrence patterns of Himalayan ibex and snow leopards by using occupancy modeling. Ibex occupancy was positively associated with rugged terrain and higher elevations and negatively associated with distance from roads. Snow leopards showed a preference for rugged habitats. The co-occurrence of these species was mediated by roads. Ibex avoided snow leopard abundant areas by shifting toward more remote locations to reduce predation risk, whereas snow leopards adaptively track these prey movements. This study suggests that protecting remote, heterogeneous landscapes is essential for sustaining mountain ecosystems and predator-prey dynamics in northern Pakistan.

title: Periodontitis as a potential contributor to lung cancer: Epidemiological evidence, proposed mechanisms, and clinical implications
abstract: Periodontitis has been proposed as a potential contributor to lung cancer (LC), but the epidemiological, mechanistic, and clinical evidence remains heterogeneous. This structured narrative review evaluates the association between periodontitis and LC, the directness of proposed biological mechanisms, and the implications for risk assessment and supportive care. Observational studies generally report positive associations, although effect estimates vary according to periodontal ascertainment, study population, and adjustment for smoking. Clinically assessed periodontitis, self-reported or administrative diagnoses, tooth loss, periodontal-associated microbial markers, and general oral microbiome profiles represent distinct exposure domains and should not be interpreted interchangeably. The absence of a clear association among lifelong never smokers and the lack of supportive Mendelian randomization evidence further limit causal inference. Human studies demonstrate oral-lower airway microbial overlap, while experimental LC models support microbiota-related inflammatory and oncogenic signaling; however, periodontal origin, directional microbial transmission, and a continuous causal pathway from periodontitis to LC have not been established. Clinically, periodontitis should not modify current eligibility for low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening, and oral or respiratory microbiome biomarkers remain investigational. Perioperative oral care has comparatively stronger evidence for reducing postoperative pulmonary infectious complications, but this benefit should not be extrapolated to tumor recurrence or survival. Overall, current evidence supports an observational association and biological plausibility, whereas independent causality and an oncologic benefit of periodontal treatment remain unproven.

title: Deep protease profiling deconvolutes protease signatures released from activated neutrophils
abstract: Dysregulated protease activity drives the progression of cancer, cardiovascular, and inflammatory diseases. Current substrate-based detection methods lack specificity, breadth, and require prior knowledge of protease content. We have advanced deep protease profiling, through differential enrichment, substrate motif, and deconvolution analyses, to provide comprehensive, unbiased, and scalable characterizations of protease activity. Phage libraries were screened against neutrophil serine proteases or activated neutrophils, and high-throughput sequencing determined cleaved peptides. Cathepsin G, neutrophil elastase, and proteinase 3 (PR3) cleaved 5,985, 5,325, and 1,285 peptides, with substrate recognition motifs that align with natural substrates. Activated neutrophil supernatants cleaved 5,166 peptides, and inhibition of serine proteases caused 95% reduction in signal. Deconvolution algorithms identified protease signatures for elastase, cathepsin G, and PR3 proportional to their levels in neutrophils. This approach enables systematic functional analysis of proteolysis, adaptable across proteases, samples, and scenarios to advance disease understanding, diagnosis, and management.

title: Regio-specific glycan expression within the mammalian brain and tumors
abstract: The mammalian brain exhibits a complex glycan code that orchestrates neural connectivity, yet the spatial organization of functionally critical modifications of glycoproteins, such as fucosylation and sialylation, remains unclear. Using novel monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) designed for glycan detection, we mapped expression of glycan epitopes with unprecedented sensitivity, revealing non-overlapping expression patterns. Combined with targeted N -/ O -glycan profiling, we found that expression of fucosylated and sialylated glycans occurs in anatomically distinct domains in both murine and human central nervous system (CNS). Key findings include fucosylated O -glycans marking brain endothelial cells, sialylated O-glycans decorating lecticans at the nodes of Ranvier, whereas the accessory olfactory bulb harbors unique fucosylated N -glycans. RNAseq and co-localization studies confirm regio-specific glycosyltransferase activity driving this partitioning. We also found that brain tumors are distinguished by upregulated expression of specific fucosylated/sialylated epitopes compared to normal tissue. The mAb-based approach uncovers regio-specific glycan expression with implications for neurodevelopment and cancer diagnostics.

title: High-risk ARGs in environmental E. coli from the Taihu Lake watershed
abstract: The global antimicrobial-resistance crisis is exacerbated by environmental bacterial reservoirs. This work investigated antibiotic-resistance genes (ARGs) carried by E. coli from 118 surface-water samples across the Taihu Lake watershed. We isolated E. coli using mTEC agar and uidA PCR and screened isolates for 92 ARGs covering 15 resistance classes. Samples from Huzhou showed higher ARG detection rates than samples from other regions, with aminoglycoside, sulfonamide, and glycopeptide resistance genes predominant. Urban sampling sites represented ARG hotspots. Co-occurrence analysis revealed associations between quinolone and aminoglycoside resistance genes, suggestive of horizontal gene transfer. Risk assessment categorized 25.3% of samples as high risk. These observations illustrate human-driven ARG pollution in local aquatic environments and support targeted surveillance and One Health-oriented mitigation strategies.

title: Inhibition of asparagine endopeptidase extends the lifespan and improves health span during aging
abstract: Asparagine endopeptidase (AEP), also known as legumain, is a lysosomal cysteine protease whose activity increases with age and contributes to age-related tissue dysfunction. We tested whether chronic AEP inhibition could slow aging phenotypes in naturally aged mice. Here, we show that chronic treatment with the AEP inhibitor #11a extended lifespan and improved health span in aged C57BL/6 mice, together with reduced frailty and improved physical and cognitive performance. #11a treatment also attenuated several senescence- and inflammation-associated readouts in multiple organs. Mechanistically, #11a treatment suppressed AEP-dependent cleavage of nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), accompanied by an increased NAD + /NADH ratio and higher SIRT1 levels. These findings support further investigation of pharmacological AEP inhibition as a strategy to promote healthy aging.

title: Chitosan-stabilized electrospun nanofiber dressings with embedded flame-made nanosilver for the treatment of resistant infections
abstract: Wound healing can be severely compromised by infections, particularly those caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa . We developed antibacterial wound dressings based on electrospun polyvinyl alcohol-chitosan nanofibers containing flame-made silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs). The 2–10 nm Ag NPs are embedded within ∼200 nm fibers, enabling a high and sustained Ag + ion release with no detectable nanoparticle release, which may help mitigate concerns associated with nanoparticle exposure. Chitosan structurally stabilizes the fibers while modulating swelling and local pH to enhance Ag + diffusion. The dressings achieved >99.9999% bacterial reduction in vitro and up to 99% ex vivo using freshly excised human skin. Crucially, the dressings maintained >90% viability of human keratinocytes and fibroblasts and showed no detectable impairment of short-term wound healing. This study introduces a scalable, safe-by-design nanofiber platform for infection-resistant and healing-compatible wound care and supports its further evaluation in preclinical studies.

title: A longitudinal study of rotenone-induced Parkinsonism in mice
abstract: Abstract Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by profound loss of dopaminergic (DA) neurons, yet the underlying mechanism remains incompletely defined. Mitochondrial toxins can induce acute degeneration of DA neurons and Parkinsonism-like phenotypes in animal models, and epidemiological studies have linked pesticide exposure to increased PD risk; however, the long-term effects of pesticide exposure remain elusive. Here, we examined both the acute and long-term effects of rotenone exposure in mice to understand PD onset, progression, and recovery. A 21-day regimen of rotenone intraperitoneal injections (2.5 mg/kg/day) induced robust Parkinsonism-like deficits by the 4 th week, including impaired locomotion, increased anxiety-like behaviors, and deficits in motor balancing and coordination. These behavioral abnormalities were accompanied by pronounced reduction in tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression and selective loss of DA neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc). Unexpectedly, these functional impairments fully resolved by 12 months, and rotenone-treated mice behaved equally well as age-matched controls. In parallel, the TH expression and DA neuron density in SNc were restored to control levels. Together, these longitudinal results demonstrate that chronic rotenone injection induces robust but reversible Parkinsonism in the acute phase, with limited long-term consequence on Parkinsonism upon toxin cessation. These findings contrast with the prevailing view that environmental pesticide exposure irreversibly drives PD and instead they reveal a substantial resilience and adaptive capacity of the nigrostriatal dopaminergic system in vivo. Highlights Chronic rotenone exposure in mice induces robust Parkinsonism-like behaviors in both motor and non-motor domains. SNc dopaminergic neurons are reduced by ∼40% at the acute phase within 4 weeks. Both motor and non-motor deficits are fully recovered by 12 months. PD-like pathological changes in the SNc are resolved by 12 months. Infographics

title: A single arm phase II trial of chidamide plus cisplatin in advanced adenoid cystic carcinoma
abstract: Systemic therapy for recurrent or metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma remains limited, and durable disease control is difficult to achieve. We conducted a prospective, single-arm phase 2 trial of chidamide, a histone deacetylase inhibitor, plus cisplatin in 24 patients with recurrent or metastatic disease. Patients received a short chidamide lead-in followed by combination therapy for up to six cycles. The study did not meet its prespecified objective response target, with a confirmed objective response rate of 13.6% among 22 efficacy-evaluable patients. However, disease control was observed in 86.4% of patients, median progression-free survival was 17.9 months, and median overall survival was 40.3 months. Toxicity was manageable, with no treatment-related deaths. These findings support further evaluation of histone deacetylase inhibitor-platinum strategies as a disease-control approach in this rare cancer, while requiring validation in larger studies.

title: Wolf-dog hybridization: Population structure confounds genetic assignment and hybrid classification
abstract: Accurate hybrid detection is increasingly important for conservation, yet genetic assignment can be strongly biased when structured populations are analyzed as if they were homogeneous. This problem is especially relevant in recolonizing systems, where individuals from differentiated source populations meet and admix. We present and evaluate a monitoring-compatible framework that accounts for population structure before testing for hybridization, without relying on reference populations from outside the study area. Using four years of routine wolf monitoring in Czechia, a Central European contact zone of differentiated lineages, we show that ignoring population structure can inflate admixture and generate false signals of hybridization. Population-specific calibration combined with independent validation resolved ambiguous assignments and provided no evidence for ongoing wolf-dog introgression within the monitored wolf population. Our results demonstrate that population structure must be explicitly considered when interpreting hybridization signals and provide a practical framework for conservation monitoring in other structured wildlife populations.

title: Microbial dynamics across commercial spaceflights of varying duration
abstract: = 6 astronauts across two commercial International Space Station (ISS) missions: Axiom 2 (10-day mission) and Axiom 3 (21-day mission). Samples included saliva, stool, urine, and body swabs from 10 anatomical sites, profiled via 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene amplicon sequencing. Gut and oral microbiomes remained stable, while skin-associated communities exhibited transient diversity shifts post-flight. Taxonomic analysis revealed individual and site-specific patterns, as well as from the spaceflight/ISS environment. Cytokine profiling from single-cell data indicated immune activation, with IL-32 and IL-16 transcripts elevated in Axiom 2 and Axiom 3. Microbiome and interleukin correlation analyses found 14 significant associations in Axiom 2 data. These findings provide an integrated view of microbiome individuality. Our study represents a descriptive comparison of two missions, informing strategies for crew health on future long-duration missions.

title: A biomarker analysis of plasma RIME and PD-L1 for stratifying first-line immunochemotherapy outcomes in advanced ESCC
abstract: Clinical benefit from first-line PD-1 inhibitor plus chemotherapy in advanced ESCC remains heterogeneous, and PD-L1 alone provides limited stratification. We evaluated plasma lncRNA RIME as a potential biomarker for stratifying first-line treatment outcomes in a multicenter cohort of patients with advanced ESCC. In the chemotherapy plus PD-1 inhibitor group, RIME-low was associated with higher ORR and better PFS/OS, whereas RIME-high was associated with poorer outcomes. Joint RIME/PD-L1 assessment further distinguished clinical benefit. Nested-model analyses showed that RIME provided non-redundant outcome information beyond PD-L1, and treatment-by-RIME interactions supported an exploratory predictive signal for ORR and PFS. Overall, plasma RIME was associated with outcome stratification and represents a potential predictive biomarker for immunochemotherapy benefit in ESCC.

title: Identification of mitophagy-related genes with diagnostic value in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis using bioinformatics analysis
abstract: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), a major cause of end-stage renal disease, involves podocyte injury and immune dysregulation. We integrated GEO transcriptomic datasets to identify 839 differentially expressed genes and 33 differential mitophagy-related genes via differential expression analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis. Machine learning identified six candidate diagnostic biomarkers, SLIRP, BLVRB, ATP6V1F, COX5B, TMEM14A, and TRMT112, with moderate-to-good discriminatory capacity across cohorts. xCell analysis revealed extensive renal immune remodeling in FSGS with expanded pro-inflammatory cells, diminished naive T cells and Tregs, and tight correlations between hub genes and immune profiles. Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis suggested a trend of downregulation of hub genes in FSGS podocytes, alongside suppressed transcriptomic signatures of mitochondrial energy metabolism and mitophagy-related pathways. qRT-PCR and western blot validated their downregulation at the whole-renal-tissue level in FSGS mouse models. These six genes may serve as diagnostic candidates and provide research clues for exploring mitophagy mechanisms in FSGS.

title: BDCA2-dependent phagocytosis enables strain-specific activation of plasmacytoid dendritic cells by lactic acid bacteria
abstract: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) detect microbial DNA via endosomal Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9), yet the mechanisms by which they selectively internalize specific bacteria remain unclear. We demonstrate that type I interferon (IFN-I) responses to lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are entirely dependent on phagocytosis and exhibit pronounced strain specificity. Among tested strains, Lactococcus lactis strain Plasma (LC-Plasma) was efficiently phagocytosed and potently induced IFN-α in both primary human pDCs and CAL-1 cells, whereas closely related strains showed minimal uptake and cytokine production. Phagocytosis was essential for TLR9-dependent IFN-α secretion. Transcriptomic and functional analyses identified BDCA2, a galactose-binding C-type lectin receptor, as a key mediator of LAB uptake. Blocking BDCA2 significantly impaired both phagocytosis and cytokine responses. BDCA2-Fc fusion proteins bound strongly to LAB. Glycan profiling identified glycan signatures associated with highly phagocytosed Lactococcus strains. These findings define BDCA2-dependent phagocytosis as a critical determinant of strain-specific LAB recognition by human pDCs.

title: An intelligent weighted adaptive regression process for reliable and uncertainty aware drought forecasting
abstract: Accurate drought forecasting enables the management and reduction of impacts on water resources and farming systems. Hence, this research introduces a hybrid machine learning model called the weighted adaptive regression process (WARP), based on Gaussian process regression, generalized ridge regression, an adaptive mechanism to dynamically update the kernel matrix, and a feature relevance mechanism to assign weights to input variables. The model is optimized using the enhanced multi-operator Runge-Kutta algorithm. Moreover, a novel feature selection method based on kernel ridge regression and permutation importance is developed, while an enhanced multi-variate variational mode decomposition is implemented to decompose the input variables. The WARP applied to forecast SPEI at three stations in Iran outperformed LSSVM, DRVFL, and CFNN with correlation coefficient of up to 0.99 and MaxAE of 0.49. The uncertainty analysis demonstrated lower uncertainty and narrower prediction intervals confirming WARP as a reliable and promising drought forecasting approach.

title: GFRAL genetic variations and circulating GFRAL in hyperemesis gravidarum
abstract: Hyperemesis gravidarum, the most severe form of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, is linked to variants in GDF15 and its receptor GFRAL . This study combined exome and targeted sequencing, genotyping, immunoassays, and clinical data to characterize GFRAL sequence variation and circulating soluble GFRAL (sGFRAL) in pregnancy. Rare GFRAL variants were identified in patients with hyperemesis gravidarum and in asymptomatic pregnancies. A common variant was associated with symptoms persisting beyond 27 weeks' gestation. sGFRAL was frequently detectable in early pregnancy, with dynamic changes across gestation and inverse correlation with weight loss, and subsequently more common in hyperemesis gravidarum. In silico promoter analysis suggested progesterone-dependent repression of GFRAL transcription, concordant with sGFRAL downregulation in controls after week 6. In contrast, women with hyperemesis gravidarum maintained soluble receptor levels. These findings implicate genetic and post-translational regulation of GFRAL in pregnancy sickness and support further evaluation of sGFRAL as a biomarker and mechanistic readout.

title: Molecular profile of micronutrient-producing microorganisms following Martian mission-relevant ionizing radiation dose rate exposure
abstract: This study evaluated the radiation tolerance, biomass production, vitamin biosynthesis, and whole-proteome response of three edible extremotolerant microorganisms, i.e., Debaryomyces hansenii DSM 3428, Bacillus subtilis DSM 10, and Limosilactobacillus reuteri DSM 20016, under a Martian mission-relevant ionizing radiation dose rate. Cultures were exposed to Martian cruise and Martian surface dose rates of gamma ionizing radiation, using γ-rays of a 60 Co source. Biomass yield and riboflavin content of irradiated cultures were analyzed. Proteomic analyses were conducted for the bacteria B. subtilis and L. reuteri , for which well-annotated reference genomes and proteomes were available. Also, post-irradiation regrowth characteristics were tested. D. hansenii and B. subtilis showed no significant impairment in growth rate post-irradiation, biomass production, or riboflavin synthesis during chronic exposure, and normal post-irradiation regrowth, similar to non-exposed cultures. In contrast, L. reuteri exhibited a higher radiation sensitivity, with a reduced biomass yield in the irradiated cultures, and an altered post-irradiation growth profile.

title: A myriad of mysteries on many legs: Disentangling the systematics of Myriapoda with UCEs
abstract: Myriapods are one of the oldest and most diverse groups of arthropods, encompassing the classes Diplopoda, Chilopoda, Symphyla, and Pauropoda. Phylogenetic analyses historically disagree on the placement and relationships of groups within the subphylum using various methodologies (i.e. morphology, Sanger sequencing, transcriptomics). Here, we develop a novel UCE (ultraconserved element) probe set for Myriapoda sampling Siphoniulida and Siphonocryptida, among the rarest millipede lineages, and explore family-level relationships within Scutigeromorpha. The probe set was tested in-vitro for 63 new specimens together with published transcriptomes and genomes totalling 23 of the 24 orders. We recovered an average of 666 loci and reconstructed a phylogeny that identifies two alternative class-level topologies, favoring Diplopoda as sister group to Pauropoda + Symphyla. We corroborate placement of Siphonocryptida within Polyzoniida and Siphoniulida as sister group to Stemmiulida. This probe set demonstrates high phylogenetic utility, allowing researchers to address outstanding questions in the field of myriapod evolution.

title: Comprehensive approach to characterize the circuit between the E and the MVL concerned with visual processing in the avian pallium
abstract: Like most mammals, birds possess advanced visual perception. However, the organization of the avian pallium is largely different from that of the mammalian layered cortex. Here, using viral tracing, the neural connectivity between the entopallium (E) and the mesopallium ventrolaterale (MVL), two visual processing regions in the pallium of the pigeon (Columba livia), was shown to be bidirectional, but dominated by E→MVL. MVL neurons projecting to E or receiving projections from E were SATB2 immunoreactive. According to single-cell RNA sequencing data, NeuronChat indicated that the strength of ligand-receptor interactions in E→MVL was weighted more heavily than that in MVL→E. Electrophysiological studies showed that MVL neurons exhibited more elongated receptive fields. Three-dimensional reconstruction for SATB2 cells in MVL receiving projection from E indicated an enrichment of mature mushroom spines in the proximal dendritic compartment. These results are helpful in deepening the understanding of the neural mechanism underlying visual processing in the avian pallium.

title: Integration of audiovisual danger stimuli in the zebrafish tectum is linked with premotor and behavioral enhancements
abstract: Multisensory integration enables animals to combine sensory cues, enhancing threat detection and escape behaviors. Although the Tectum is traditionally considered a visual center, its role in integrating auditory and visual danger signals is not fully understood. Using in vivo calcium imaging in larval zebrafish, we demonstrate that auditory stimuli recruit a significant population of tectal neurons, mainly in deep layers. Visual looms elicit strong tectal responses, but combined auditory-visual stimuli robustly increase neural activity and the likelihood of rapid escape, especially for less salient cues engaging more tectal neurons than unisensory stimuli. These results establish the zebrafish Tectum as a multisensory processing area. Notably, the heightened tectal response during multisensory stimulation is strongly correlated with increased activity in hindbrain neurons implicated in escape-like motion events, connecting tectal integration to premotor circuits that drive behavioral output. Our findings provide a mechanistic basis for tectal multisensory processing in enhancing behavioral escape responses.

title: WTAP-mediated m6A methylation stabilizes pIgR mRNA and attenuates smoke-induced epithelial inflammation and apoptosis
abstract: Smoke inhalation injury (SII) dramatically elevates burn patient mortality. Although N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methylation is emerging as a central epitranscriptomic regulator of lung inflammation and injury, its specific involvement in SII remains unknown. Using an in vivo mouse SII model and smoke extract-treated MLE-12 cells, we show that smoke exposure downregulates the m6A writer-complex component WTAP and reduces global m6A methylation. WTAP knockdown attenuates epithelial inflammation, apoptosis, and STAT3 activation. Integrating transcriptomics with weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and MeRIP-qPCR, we identify pIgR as a downstream target: WTAP modifies m6A methylation within the 756/772 region of pIgR mRNA, and its knockdown prolongs pIgR mRNA half-life and elevates pIgR expression. pIgR silencing reverses the protection conferred by WTAP knockdown. These findings define a WTAP/m6A/pIgR axis that shapes the early epithelial response to smoke inhalation and identifies WTAP as a candidate therapeutic target for SII.

title: The NeuroEpiTool—A digital tool to ascertain neurological outcomes in population-based studies
abstract: Background: Collecting data on signs and symptoms of neurological disorders is especially relevant in neuroepidemiological fieldwork. However, it typically requires extensive specialised training, limiting accessibility in resource-constrained settings. This study aimed to develop and internally validate the NeuroEpiTool, a digital tool designed to facilitate data collection in neuroepidemiological studies without requiring a neurologist.

title: Perceptual lengthening of visual time throughout learning of hand-reaching actions
abstract: Abstract Timing is intimately woven into human cognition and behaviour, underscoring people’s ability of comprehending speech, playing instruments and competing in sports. Converging evidence suggests that our perceptual experience of time is grounded in our ability to control actions: time processing leverages motor control neural machinery, and perceived time is significantly distorted in proximity of action. However, the dynamic interplay between timing and action systems remains unexplored, particularly in goal-directed contexts where action control is gradually refined through practice. Through combined behavioural, neural and modelling approaches, we investigate how time processing gradually evolves as participants gain experience in goal-driven manual reaching actions, varying in terms of action-plan specificity. Participants judged brief visual durations while preparing hand movements aimed at visual targets displayed on a monitor. Subjective time expanded in the foreperiod preceding action onset, and this effect increased over trials, mirroring gradual improvements in action readiness as motor plans became more rapidly and efficiently deployed. Representation Similarity Analysis, integrating electroencephalographic and behavioural data, reveals that actions shape timing through independent mechanisms: planning specific behaviours shapes how duration information is written into timekeeping neural circuits as stimuli unfold (encoding). Parallely, more general aspects of motor engagement and anticipation shape how duration information is read-out from timing circuits following stimulus presentation (decoding). These findings highlight a dynamic, learning-driven coupling between perceptual time and motor control, where subjective time is recalibrated as goal-directed action preparation is optimized, shaped through independent time encoding and decoding mechanisms. Significance statement Despite lacking dedicated sensory and neural systems for duration, humans reveal a highly developed ‘sense’ of time, for instance when noticing subtle tempo changes in music. We show that perceptual understanding of time is linked to the ability of learning and fine-tuning action: our internal metric of time shifts as action preparation processes are gradually refined, affecting how quickly behaviours are planned and executed. This interaction is mediated by independent neural processes affecting the encoding (online monitoring) and decoding (offline readout) of duration. These findings shift our understanding of timing, from a passive sensory readout to one that is actively constructed and finetuned through action learning, and provide a mechanistic account of neural processes linking action preparation to time processing

title: Maternal gut microbiota, tryptophan metabolism and immune homeostasis: Implications for the prevention of adverse pregnancy complications
abstract: The gut microbiota critically regulates host metabolism and immunity, and its dysbiosis disrupts immune homeostasis during pregnancy, increasing risks of preeclampsia, preterm birth, and fetal growth restriction. This review synthesizes current evidence on how maternal gut microbiota and their metabolites—particularly tryptophan (Trp) catabolites—orchestrate immune adaptations essential for fetal tolerance. We summarize the dynamic remodeling of gut microbial communities across gestation and discuss how dysbiosis impairs pregnancy immunity through disrupted Trp metabolism. Importantly, we highlight Trp-derived metabolites (kynurenine, serotonin, and indole derivatives) as key signaling molecules linking the gut microbiota to immune checkpoints, including the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) and indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) pathways, which modulate Treg/Th17 balance and placental barrier integrity. By integrating perspectives from immunology, microbiology, and reproductive biology, this framework positions microbial Trp metabolism as a promising therapeutic target for preventing gestational complications and improving maternal-infant health.

title: Toll-like receptor 4-driven translational reprogramming in macrophages is unaffected by Salmonella SPI-1 activity
abstract: Changes in gene expression during bacterial infection are the combined result of altered transcription and translation, with the latter comparatively understudied. Gram-negative bacteria rapidly trigger cytokine gene transcription in macrophages through the activation of pathogen-associated molecular pattern receptors, for example the detection of Salmonella lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from the bacterial cell envelope by Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). Here, through time-resolved parallel translatomic and transcriptomic profiling, we now show temporal TLR4-specific translational upregulation of cell signaling proteins in macrophages induced by Salmonella . While transcriptional upregulation of these genes is dampened through the activity of the Salmonella SPI-1 type 3 secretion system, a robust translational response remains. These data reveal an important host-pathogen translational regulatory network that modifies the innate immune response of macrophages to infection.

title: CK2 and DBT promote temperature compensation of the Drosophila circadian clock via distinct pathways
abstract: Abstract Circadian (∼24 h) rhythms are essential for the survival of most organisms, as they optimize physiology and behavior with the time of day. They are defined by three fundamental properties: they are driven by a self-sustained molecular oscillator, entrained by environmental cues such as light and temperature, and temperature-compensated, whereby circadian period remains close to 24 h over a physiological range of temperatures. The molecular basis of temperature compensation remains incompletely understood. Here, we build on previous studies supporting a conserved and important role for phosphorylation-dependent mechanisms in the control of temperature compensation. We found that reducing the activity of two highly conserved circadian kinases, DBT (casein kinase [CK] 1) and CK2, disrupts temperature compensation in Drosophila .
